claims.text: A hybrid methodology can train high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potentials on ab initio molecular-dynamics data.
The training data and resulting potential can explicitly retain electron–vibration coupling and anharmonic effects.
Deploying the machine-learning potential in enhanced-sampling free-energy integration can compute the free energies of both solid and liquid phases.
Umbrella sampling or metadynamics are suitable accelerated integration schemes for the proposed solid–liquid free-energy calculation.
The machine-learning-derived potential-energy surface will accurately capture atomic interactions, vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
Interatomic potentials can reproduce selected first-principles and experimental properties in a multicomponent high-entropy alloy.
A machine-learning potential that reproduces the ab initio energy landscape will permit substantially cheaper phase-space sampling.
Enhanced sampling with the machine-learning potential will accelerate convergence of free-energy calculations by reducing the amount of explicit ab initio molecular dynamics required.
The reduced-cost workflow will maintain fidelity to full quantum-mechanical behavior.
The method will accurately predict fusion free energies and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
Phase free energies and derived observables will differ from explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results by only a few meV per atom.
The method will be approximately 10–100 times faster than explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
For multicomponent systems, the method will be approximately 2–5 times faster than TOR-TILD.
The workflow can first be validated for elemental and binary systems near their melting points.
After elemental or binary validation, the workflow can be extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Conventional computational studies of high-entropy alloys are limited by the availability of suitable force fields.
The intended operating regime is at or above the melting point, where vibrational and electronic entropy contributions are critical.
Training-data quality and sampling efficiency may cause system-dependent deviations in accuracy and speed.
Latent heat and melting temperature can be derived from the calculated solid and liquid phase free energies.
